title: Unmasking Superficial Charm: Defining and Measuring it in the Social Context
abstract: This thesis explores the behavioural, contextual, and perceptual foundations of superficial charm, presenting a reconceptualisation of charm as a multidimensional, context-sensitive, and socially regulated construct. Across six empirical studies, it develops and tests the Superficial Charm Measure (SCM), which differentiates superficial charm into three core behavioural dimensions: Performed Social Fluency, Strategic and Instrumental, and Genuine Prosocial. These factors reflect distinct, but interacting, modes of charm expression, ranging from emotionally sincere and affiliative behaviours to those that are strategically motivated and manipulative. Using a multi-method approach—including qualitative thematic analysis, psychometric scale development, facial expression analysis, and interaction paradigms—this research examines how charm is broadcast, perceived, and interpreted across interpersonal contexts. Study 1 used qualitative interviews to identify behavioural traits associated with both charm and superficial charm, forming the foundation for item development. Studies 2 and 3 refined and tested the three-factor structure of the SCM. Studies 4 through 6 examined contextual moderators of charm perception, including social power, sex, observer bias, and the distinction between third-party observers and direct recipients. Key findings demonstrate that sex, social power, and target familiarity with the charmer significantly influence how charm is interpreted. The findings position superficial charm as a norm-driven, strategic, and co-constructed interpersonal behaviour. It is a measurable, socially embedded phenomenon that lies at the intersection of authenticity, influence and deception. Additionally, the development of the candidate measure, the SCM, contributes a novel tool to clinical, forensic, organisational, and interpersonal contexts, as well as the study of social influence, impression management, and social perception—although further validation is required.

title: Facilitators and Barriers Influencing Patient Safety Activities in Long-Term Care Facilities: An Integrative Review Guided by the SEIPS 101 Model.
abstract: Nurses' patient safety activities in long-term care facilities (LTCFs) are influenced by systemic factors within complex work systems. Despite increasing attention to patient safety in LTCFs, comprehensive syntheses that specifically examine facilitators and barriers influencing nurses' patient safety activities within an established theoretical framework remain limited. This integrative review synthesized evidence on facilitators and barriers influencing nurses' patient safety activities in LTCFs using the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) 101 model. The literature search covered publications from January 1, 2010, to June 12, 2025, across CINAHL, PubMed, ProQuest, and MEDLINE, along with two domestic databases (Korean Studies Information Service System and Research Information Sharing Service). The review followed the five-step integrative review framework and was reported according to the PRISMA guidelines. Two independent reviewers conducted data extraction and methodological quality appraisal using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, and the review protocol was registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/RH6KX). Twenty studies met the inclusion criteria. The findings identified the "socio-organizational environment" domain as both the predominant facilitator and barrier, followed by the "people" and "tasks" domains, which were more frequently reported as barriers than facilitators. The synthesis demonstrates that patient safety activities in LTCFs are shaped by dynamic feedback loops among the work systems, work processes, and work outcomes, rather than by isolated nursing activities. The proposed framework based on the SEIPS 101 model provides a foundation for developing targeted guidelines and intervention strategies to strengthen patient safety activities among nurses in LTCFs.

title: Self-organizing social systems: boundaries of cooperation and coordination
abstract: Networked problem solving underlies the formative dynamics of a variety of complex systems. In this setting it is important to consider not just what network ties exist, but how ties change over time, and the influence this has on the behavior and exchange facilitated by these interactions. Ranging from cellular communication to human organization, collectives engage in goal-oriented behavior and adapt to maximize their rewards. When considering a network tie between two problem solvers, optimal group-level outcomes often depend on two overarching concepts: cooperation and coordination. The first two projects of this dissertation use stylized models of networked problem solvers to demonstrate how preferential interaction (i.e., adapting network ties to maximize individual rewards) can lead to distinct system dynamics. In one setting, preferential interaction is shown to harm cooperative prosocial behaviors, while in the other it promotes coordination and robustness. The first agent-based model demonstrates the conditions under which spiteful behavior could emerge. Spite is a behavior that harms both the actor and recipient, and therefore its emergence is evolutionarily counterintuitive. The model demonstrates that if agents are able to interact preferentially, spiteful behavior can gain a relative advantage and become the norm in a population. A second agent-based model examines the formation of signaling conventions under preferential interaction. This is the first model to demonstrate agents' use of a novel form of signaling, where communicating partners failed to reach a consensus on the meaning of each signal. Instead, agents solved the signaling problem by using the network structure to ensure two distinct types of complementary signaling strategies interacted. Finally, the third project reports on an online survey and experiment conducted on an online labor market platform. This project examines the psychological willingness of freelancers to cooperate in temporary teams, and how our results can inform platform design aimed at strengthening the social ties between freelancers. Our results suggest that our freelance participants display traits that are more consistent with belonging to a shared, coherent group than would be expected given existing theory. Overall, the chapters of this dissertation consider self-organization in game theoretic and real-world settings, and show how emergent behaviors are influenced type of relational links that form. --Author's abstract

title: Roles of empathy in altruistic cooperation in adults with and without autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Altruistic cooperation (AC) is essential in human social interactions. Previous studies have investigated AC-related behavior in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), revealing that there is considerable individual variability in the behavior. However, this issue is still largely unexplored especially in the adult population. To investigate individual differences in AC-related behavior, we conducted the resource allocation task (RAT) and modified version of the ultimatum game (mUG) among adults with and without ASD. The study employed a cross-sectional design, involving 27 adults with ASD (mean age 29.1 ± 4.3 years; three females) and 27 adults with typical development (TD) (mean age 25.8 ± 6.7 years; two females), who completed the RAT and mUG tasks. Beyond clinical characteristics, we assessed three primary psychological metrics: the interpersonal reactivity index (IRI), Barratt impulsiveness scale, and the behavioral inhibition and activation systems. No significant differences were observed in the proportions of participants with high AC when assessed by RAT (p = 0.15) and mUG (p = 0.59) between the TD and ASD groups. Participants with high AC from the RAT demonstrated higher perspective-taking scores on the IRI than those with low AC within both the TD (p = 0.04) and ASD groups (p = 0.03). In the TD group, high AC individuals also scored higher on the IRI's fantasy subscale as per the mUG (p = 0.03); however, this trend was not present in the ASD group. The present findings indicate that empathy plays an important role in individual differences in AC-related behavior among adults with and without ASD, although the role could be different depending on the types of AC-related behavior between TD and ASD populations.

title: Development and preliminary evaluation of a WeChat mini-program-based mobile pharmacy management assistance system in a Chinese women and Children's hospital.
abstract: Traditional pharmacy management, which relies on paper- and computer-based methods, is often inefficient and inflexible. There is an urgent need to develop support tools to address these challenges. The WeChat mini-program has been applied in multiple fields because it is readily accessible within the WeChat ecosystem. Its use in pharmacy management may support more accessible and flexible workflows. To develop and evaluate a WeChat mini-program-based Mobile Pharmacy Management Assistance System. A Pharmacy Collaboration Team consisting of front-line pharmacists, pharmacy administrators, and one informatics pharmacist was established to collect functional requirements through group discussions. The system was developed as a WeChat mini-program and implemented in routine pharmacy-management practice. After the 3-month implementation period, participating pharmacists were invited to complete a questionnaire. The questionnaire included the System Usability Scale, self-reported experience ratings comparing paper-based, computer-based, and mobile management modes, and open-ended feedback. Experience ratings were summarized using medians and interquartile ranges. Differences among the three paired management modes were analyzed using the Friedman test with Bonferroni correction. The final version of the system consisted of six modules: shift handovers, drug knowledge base, medication-error recording and analysis, drug-expiry reminders, damaged-drug recording, and medication consultations. Twenty-eight participants were invited to participate, and 27 completed valid questionnaires. The mean System Usability Scale score was 79.54 with a standard deviation of 11.33. The mobile-based mode received higher ratings for accessibility, work data sharing, and update frequency. The most frequently selected liked feature was the convenience of access anytime and anywhere, whereas the least appreciated feature was the limited interface size on mobile devices. This single-center exploratory evaluation supports the feasibility and preliminary usability of a WeChat mini-program-based mobile pharmacy management assistance system developed through a multi-role Pharmacy Collaboration Team. The system showed potential advantages in selected self-reported user-experience dimensions among pharmacists. However, the findings should be interpreted as preliminary evidence based on perceived user experience. Larger multicenter studies using objective workflow, data-quality, and medication-management outcomes are needed to evaluate its practical impact further.

title: Video Games and Players’ Empathy, Compassion, and Sympathy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Due to the importance of empathy, the popularity of video games, and the potential contributions to the Differential Susceptibility to Media Effects Model (DSMM), this thesis examined the relationship between video games and empathy-related constructs, including compassion and sympathy. Based on 84 previous studies, this systematic review revealed associations between video games and empathy-related constructs, as well as the diversity in the empathy-related concepts measured by scholars and the instruments used to measure these concepts. A meta-analysis based on 18 studies supported the superior positive impact of prosocial gaming content on players' state empathy, compared to violent video games, neutral video games, and other formats of education such as reading textbooks. This synthesis and integration of research findings support both existing and new propositions for the DSMM

title: Price Transparency and Patient Engagement: Social Messaging Matters
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the effects of price transparency and prosocial messaging on price-protected consumers' health care choices as a potential cost-saving strategy to manage rising US health care expenditures. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. Participants were recruited to complete a basic questionnaire via Amazon's Mechanical Turk program. Participants' selections were subsequently collected and analyzed. METHODS: Participants (N = 567) selected a sleep study provider from 5 options, with manipulations including financial responsibility, provision of price information, and a prosocial message encouraging high-value options. RESULTS: Price transparency increased the selection of lower-cost options among participants who were solely responsible for paying for their own health care expenses. For participants whose insurance paid for health care expenses, both price transparency and prosocial messaging were necessary to choose lower-cost options. CONCLUSIONS: The study highlights the importance of considering both financial and social factors in patient engagement initiatives, suggesting that a combination of price transparency and prosocial messaging can influence health care choices and potentially contribute to cost-saving strategies in the US health care system.

title: Pediatric palliative care research participation: do adolescent and adult patients and caregivers find it acceptable?
abstract: Palliative care has matured as a life-span field with an increasing research base. Advancing the field means understanding why patients and caregivers participate in palliative care research, and participation's benefits and burdens. This study extended previous work to include greater diversity of clinical sampling and study design. Prospective, multi-methods study examined reported benefits, burdens, and motivations associated with participation in pediatric palliative care research. Study pParticipants included patients, caregivers, and family members who enrolled in pediatric palliative care research, as well as individuals declining participation, within a single quaternary pediatric hospital system. Structured questionnaires were administered at enrollment and study completion; qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. 57 participants completed the questionnaires. Altruism and personal benefit were the most frequently cited motivations for enrollment at baseline and study completion. Emotional expression and the opportunity to help others were commonly identified as positive aspects of participation. The majority reported no discomfort and indicated willingness to participate in future research. The most frequent reasons given for declining participation were feeling overwhelmed, lack of interest, or study-specific aversion, rather than distress associated with palliative care research iPPC involvement. Participants consistently reported greater benefit than burden, suggesting that pediatric palliative care research participation is acceptable and often meaningful. Given the pre/post design, the findings suggest eligible participants are able to determine if actual study participation is likely beneficial for them or not. Supporting families as they consider research participation promotes ethical, sensitive, and inclusive research design. Identified patterns may guide research design for future investigators to continue to advance the science of pediatric palliative care across the lifespanresearch.

title: Meanings mothers attribute to caring for children with congenital toxoplasmosis: A virtual ethnography on Facebook®.
abstract: Congenital toxoplasmosis is a significant public health concern due to its severity and its profound impact on maternal and family care. To explore how mothers of children with congenital toxoplasmosis use Facebook to share caregiving experiences and construct meanings related to their maternal trajectories within digital support networks. This is an exploratory, qualitative study based on virtual ethnography. The study followed six methodological steps: participant search, group characterization, data collection, interviews, transcription, and analysis. Seventeen Facebook® spaces, including personal accounts, pages, and groups, were analyzed, addressing topics such as birth narratives, diagnosis, sequelae, family impact, spirituality, and emotions. Subsequently, interviews were conducted with seven mothers. The results were organized into three thematic categories: (1) the impact of the diagnosis on family life and the search for information; (2) the resources mobilized by mothers to cope with atypical motherhood, such as social support, faith, and welcoming networks; and (3) the everyday uses of Facebook, with emphasis on visibility strategies, care with exposure, and the construction of belonging. Initially, mothers turned to virtual groups seeking support and information, later moving on to sharing their own experiences on personal profiles and other platforms. The findings highlight the importance of understanding the emotional and informational needs of mothers of children with congenital toxoplasmosis, emphasizing the value of promoting welcoming and collaborative spaces in digital environments that foster mutual support and experience sharing.

title: Understanding the Role of Peer Support in Managing Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis: A Qualitative Study among Dutch Young Adults
abstract: A chronic disease, such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), can significantly impact a young adult’s life. While peer support has been recognised as a valuable resource for managing the challenges of a chronic disease, limited research exists on its specific role for young adults with JIA. In this qualitative study, 11 participants (aged 18–30, diagnosed with JIA) were interviewed on how they perceived and utilised peer support in managing their condition. Young adults with JIA highlighted the crucial role of peer support to provide emotional support (e.g., understanding of experiences), informational support (e.g., practical advice and problem-solving strategies) and appraisal support (e.g., normalisaton of experiences). Our findings emphasise that peer support fulfils a distinct and complementary role within a broader support system, alongside professional support and support from family and friends, together addressing both the physical and psychosocial needs of young adults with JIA.

title: The relevance of top-down self-regulation for children's and adolescents' developmental outcomes.
abstract: A popular topic in developmental science is self-regulation, an aspect of functioning viewed as contributing to optimal development. Of particular theoretical importance is top-down (frontal cortically based) self-regulation (TDSR). This article briefly reviews recent research on TDSR's relation to four areas of development: maladjustment, social competence, prosocial development, and academic development. Recent studies on the topic often involve sophisticated methods and designs; moreover, several relevant meta-analyses have been published in the recent past. In general, a higher level of TDSR has been associated with better adjustment, social competence, prosociality, and success in the school setting. Limitations in the research and extant meta-analyses are briefly noted.

title: Social Robots and Children’s Development: Promises and Implications
abstract: Social robots are increasingly ubiquitous in children’s lives, prompting questions regarding the promise and implications for children’s development. Social robots can be effective and helpful technological tools. Social robots are effective in supporting children’s learning in some domains, supporting better learning outcomes than with virtual agents and comparable to human tutors when tasks are simple and social. They also support the unique and individual needs of children with a range of special needs (e.g., autism spectrum disorder, hearing impairment) and promote children’s mental well-being and physical health. Yet social robots pose conceptual and ethical challenges in that they often present as if they have psychological and social characteristics. Consequently, children often understand social robots as mental, social, and moral entities, albeit to varying degrees depending upon children’s ages and robots’ features. Moreover, children treat robots in prosocial ways (e.g., helping, sharing) and believe robots deserve moral treatment. Yet, at the same time, some children deliberately abuse robots. Future research is needed to address critical questions and guide recommendations for the promise and limitations of social robots in children’s lives.

title: Syrian Refugee Women's Contraception Preferences and Factors Influencing Decision-Making: A Qualitative Study in Türkiye.
abstract: We aimed to assess the knowledge of Syrian refugee women living in Türkiye regarding contraception, identify their preferred methods, and investigate factors influencing decision-making. From June to July 2023, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 Syrian refugee women attending an outpatient clinic in Samsun, Türkiye. We analyzed transcripts for content and themes to identify findings regarding preferences and barriers. Early marriage (as young as 13) and high fertility (up to 10 children) were prevalent among our participants. Attitudes toward contraception were divided between a pragmatic approach-viewing contraception as a means to achieve "peace of mind," economic stability, and better childcare-and socioreligious fatalism, where children are seen as "gifts from God" and interference is considered morally impermissible (haram). Although the intrauterine device and oral contraceptive pills were the most recognized methods, side effects such as heavy bleeding and irritability led to high discontinuation rates. Information generally flowed from social networks and social media due in part to the lack of Arabic-speaking healthcare staff in the area. Our findings suggest substantial structural and socio-cultural barriers prevent effective contraceptive use among Syrian refugees in Samsun, Türkiye. Addressing these gaps requires linguistically and culturally sensitive services, including the employment of Arabic-speaking female staff. Proactive information sharing is essential to dispel myths and manage expectations regarding contraceptive side effects.

title: Early social-cognitive development as a dynamic developmental system—a lifeworld approach
abstract: Based on developmental systems and dynamic systems theories, we propose the lifeworld approach-a conceptual framework for research and a hypothesis concerning early social-cognitive development. As a framework, the lifeworld approach recognizes the social embeddedness of development and shifts the focus away from individual developmental outcomes toward the reciprocal interplay of processes within and between individuals that co-constitutes early social-cognitive development. As a hypothesis, the lifeworld approach proposes that the changing developmental system-spanning the different individuals as their subsystems-strives toward attractor states through regulation at the behavioral level, which results in both the emergence and further differentiation of developmental attainments. The lifeworld approach-as a framework and a hypothesis, including key methodological approaches to test it-is exemplified by research on infants' self-awareness, prosocial behavior and social learning. Equipped with, first, a conceptual framework grounded in a modern view on development and, second, a growing suite of methodological approaches, developmental science can advance by analyzing the mutually influential relations between intra-individual and interactional processes in order to identify key mechanisms underlying early social-cognitive development.

title: Designing History-Based Educational Games to Improve Cognitive Empathy in Children with ASD: A Pilot Study
abstract: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) face significant challenges in Theory of Mind (ToM), particularly in understanding others' perspectives. While serious games have shown potential, most existing interventions focus on basic emotion recognition without engaging narrative contexts. Objective: This pilot study aims to design a history-based serious game, "Tarumanegara Adventure," and evaluate its preliminary effectiveness in improving cognitive empathy among children with high-functioning ASD. Using a mixed-methods case study approach with a one-group pretest - post-test design, six students with ASD (aged 8-15) participated in a 2-week intervention. The game integrates historical narratives as a logical scaffold with explicit emotion scaffolding and moral decision-making mechanics. Data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test and triangulated with behavioral observations. Quantitative results showed a significant increase in cognitive empathy scores (p = 0.0312) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 3.19). However, triangulation revealed a "knowing-doing gap," in which higher cognitive scores did not correlate significantly with spontaneous prosocial behavior (ρ = -0.36). Conclusion: The history-based narrative approach effectively enhances cognitive knowledge of empathy by providing a structured context. However, bridging the gap between cognitive understanding and spontaneous behavioral application remains a critical challenge for future game design.

title: Design, Validation, and Reliability Study of the Social Capital Scale for Parents.
abstract: The Purpose of this study was to develop the Social Capital Scale for Parents (SCSP), to test its reliability and validity. The research used a correlational design. Data were collected from two independent samples: 295 parents for Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and 121 parents for Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). The EFA indicated that the SCSP includes three subscales: Capital in Social Interaction, Trust Capital, and Altruistic Capital, and Confirmatory Factor Analysis showed good fit indices. As a result of the reliability analysis, it was observed that the overall Cronbach's Alpha internal consistency coefficient was .85, and McDonald's Omega coefficient was .89. Based on these results, it was concluded that the scale can produce reliable and valid measures of parents' social capital.

title: Television content exposure in toddlerhood: Profiles, predictors, and developmental correlates in New Zealand
abstract: Television viewing is a common feature of early childhood, including toddlerhood; however, evidence regarding the developmental implications of different types of television content in toddlerhood remains limited. The present study examined television viewing in two-year-old children across seven content dimensions, including pace, prosocial content, antisocial and aggressive content, educational strategies, depictions of emotions, mental state talk, and cultural consciousness. Data from 5,338 two-year-old children and their mothers was obtained from the prospective, longitudinal Growing Up in New Zealand study. Latent profile analysis was used to identify five distinct profiles with regards to child media content exposure. Children with certain pre-disposing factors such as negative emotionality and within certain contexts, including less educated parents and fewer screen media rules in place, were more likely to be exposed to content containing high levels of antisocial content presented in a visually fast-paced fashion. Exposure to fast-paced, antisocial content at age 2 was then in turn associated with higher levels of peer problems and emotional symptoms and lower vocabulary and affective knowledge at age 4. Findings highlight the importance of considering both quantity and quality when evaluating the impacts of early childhood media use.

title: Personality testing of large language models: limited temporal stability, but highlighted prosociality
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) continue to gain popularity due to their human-like traits and the intimacy they offer to users, their societal impact inevitably expands. This leads to the rising necessity for comprehensive studies to fully understand LLMs and reveal their potential opportunities, drawbacks and overall societal impact. With that in mind, this research conducted an extensive investigation into seven LLMs, aiming to assess the temporal stability and inter-rater agreement on their responses on personality instruments in two time points. In addition, LLMs' personality profile was analysed and compared with human normative data. The findings revealed varying levels of inter-rater agreement in the LLMs' responses over a short time, with some LLMs showing higher agreement (e.g. Llama3 and GPT-4o) compared with others (e.g. GPT-4 and Gemini). Furthermore, agreement depended on used instruments as well as on domain or trait. This implies the variable robustness in LLMs' ability to reliably simulate stable personality characteristics. In the case of scales which showed at least fair agreement, LLMs displayed mostly a socially desirable profile in both agentic and communal domains, as well as a prosocial personality profile reflected in higher agreeableness and conscientiousness and lower Machiavellianism. Exhibiting temporal stability and coherent responses on personality traits is crucial for AI systems due to their societal impact and AI safety concerns.

title: Why are younger-age adults reluctant to give blood? A reflexive thematic analysis of non-donors in the United Kingdom
abstract: The present study explored the psychosocial factors influencing blood donation behaviour among younger-age adults classified as non-donors in the United Kingdom. Six participants (aged 18–35) with no history of blood donation were recruited via opportunity sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify key patterns in participant narratives related to donation behaviour. Two overarching themes were identified. Barriers to blood donation included four sub-themes: (i) socially constructed misconceptions of eligibility and need, (ii) embodied discomfort and perceived invasiveness of the donation process, (iii) disengagement and deferred responsibility in blood donation, and (iv) perceived absence and inaccessibility of blood donation campaigns. Facilitators of blood donation included three sub-themes: (i) promoting blood donation by addressing diverse reward preferences, (ii) the importance of procedural clarity in reducing uncertainty, and (iii) increasing motivation to donate blood through cues to act. Tailored public health strategies must address adult non-donors’ psychological and informational barriers, including misconceptions, procedural uncertainty, and anxiety about physical reactions. Interventions should pair targeted communication with accessible, accurate information and frame donation as both socially beneficial and personally rewarding.

title: Path to Prevention Platform Trial in Early-Stage Neuronal Alpha-Synuclein Disease: Study Design.
abstract: The development of biologically targeted therapeutics (BTTs) that slow Parkinson's disease progression has been hampered by a reliance on testing interventions in clinically defined populations with already advanced pathobiology. Publications on the biological definition and classification of neuronal α-synuclein disease (NSD), and the development of the NSD integrated staging system (NSD-ISS), have generated a framework for identifying individuals with NSD prior to the emergence of a clinically defined syndrome. Path to Prevention (P2P) is a phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled platform trial designed to assess the safety and efficacy of interventions in an early-stage NSD population. The trial is embedded within the observational Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a structure that enables recruitment of participants from the PPMI cohort, leverages existing operational infrastructure, and utilizes data from non-P2P enrolled PPMI participants in the Bayesian statistical modeling. P2P will enroll participants at least 60 years of age with NSD Stage 2B (abnormal α-synuclein, dopaminergic dysfunction, and prodromal signs or symptoms without functional impairment) without a clinically defined diagnosis of PD or a related disorder. As a platform trial, P2P will enable the testing of multiple interventions under a Master Protocol at approximately 35 sites across North America and Europe. Interventions are selected from industry-submitted applications based on biological relevance of the targets, and on the adequacy of the safety data appropriate to the target population. Each treatment regimen will have 125 participants on active treatment and at least 125 shared placebo control participants. Participants will remain on treatment for a maximum of 144 weeks or until 96 weeks since the randomization of the last participant. P2P has two primary endpoints, 1) rate of change in mean putamen specific binding ratio from baseline through follow-up and, 2) rate of change in the MDS-UPDRS Part III motor examination from baseline through follow-up or initiation of dopaminergic treatment. A range of secondary and exploratory biomarker-focused endpoints will be assessed. The protocol was developed with input from multiple stakeholders, including people with early-stage NSD, biopharmaceutical industry leaders, and regulatory authorities. P2P is the first trial to test biologically targeted assets in biologically defined prodromal participants utilizing an efficient platform design, which will provide the field with tools to expand therapeutic development, and enable intervention at earlier stages of neurodegeneration. P2P is scheduled to begin enrollment in December 2026 and is committed to data sharing and broad dissemination of learnings from the study.

title: Supporting FAIR Practices In Scholarly Publishing with the Editorial Reference Handbook.
abstract: The Editorial Reference Handbook assists scholarly publishers in supporting the sharing of digital research objects and in operationalising FAIR research practices by addressing gaps in editorial workflows, policy implementation and stakeholder alignment. Comprising a checklist, detailed guidance, and a flowchart, the Handbook provides a flexible framework for in-house editorial staff while also providing value to reviewers, authors, and service providers. The project was developed through a co-creation process involving 14 journals and 9 publishers, and was subsequently piloted by 6 journals across 190 manuscripts. In total, 35 participants representing 19 journals and 11 publishers contributed to the various stages of the project. Evaluation through surveys and performance metrics showed that the Handbook can help in-house editorial staff ensure that data underpinning publications is shared more FAIRly without significantly impacting turnaround times or author correspondence. This article reports on the contributions of the participants, describes the rationale and development of the Handbook, and presents the outcomes of the pilot, offering a reusable framework adaptable across diverse publishing contexts.

title: Encouraging Ethical and Practical Local Government Managers: How the ICMA Code of Ethics Promotes Servant Leadership
abstract: This study empirically examined the association between the adoption of ethical codes and servant leadership in local government organizations. Analyzing survey data from the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) from 2012-2018, along with the U.S. Census Bureau’s Community Engagement and Volunteering Supplement (CEVS) to the 2021 Current Population Survey (CPS), this study explored how the associations between adoption, scope, and enforcement mechanism of ethical codes impacted seven categories of servant leadership: relationships with elected officials, policy collaboration, information exchange, innovation, performance effectiveness, service delivery, and public/community engagement. This study also explored the relationship between ethics training and these seven dimensions of servant leadership. Although evidence suggests that compliance-based ethics infrastructure such as ethical code adoption and a broadly-applying ethical code scope is associated with servant leadership, integrity-based ethics initiatives, namely a robust, continuous ethics training program, shows the strongest association with servant leadership outcomes in local government.

title: 24-h movement behavior composition associated with mental health in preschool children: a cross-sectional compositional data analysis.
abstract: Mental health problems in preschool children represent an important public health concern. Understanding the associations between 24-h movement behaviors, including moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA), light physical activity (LPA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep (SLP), and mental health may help identify activity compositions associated with more favorable psychological outcomes. This study aimed to examine the associations between reallocations of time among 24-h movement behaviors and mental health in preschool children aged 3-6 years and to identify activity compositions associated with more favorable mental health outcomes. This cross-sectional study included 850 Chinese preschool children aged 3-6 years. MVPA, LPA, and SB were objectively measured using ActiGraph GT3X-BT accelerometers, whereas SLP was assessed using structured parent- and teacher-reported questionnaires. Mental health outcomes, including total difficulties, internalizing and externalizing problems, and prosocial behavior, were assessed using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Compositional data analysis (CoDA) was performed using isometric log-ratio (ilr) transformations and multiple linear regression models. A one-to-three proportional time-reallocation approach was used to estimate changes in mental health outcomes associated with reallocating 10% of time in one behavior proportionally across the remaining three behaviors. In addition, optimal time-use analysis was conducted to identify 24-h movement compositions associated with more favorable mental health outcomes. Models were adjusted for age, gender, body mass index, residential district, parental education, and parental attitudes toward physical activity. An increase in MVPA was significantly associated with a reduction in Total Difficulties ( Greater relative time spent in MVPA and SLP was associated with more favorable mental health outcomes among preschool children. The model-derived 24-h movement behavior composition identified in this study reflects associations within the observed sample and should not be interpreted as a causal relationship or a prescriptive intervention target. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to validate these findings.

title: Mental health among children and youngsters in Kosovo
abstract: Background: Child and adolescent mental health remains under-researched and insufficiently addressed in many developing countries, including Kosovo, highlighting the need to consider the influence of social and cultural dynamics. Objective: The current study investigated the mental health of children and adolescents, taking into account the social and cultural factors that may influence their well-being. Methods: A mixed-methods design, equally weighted, was employed. The quantitative study included 318 participants. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. The qualitative study included 36 participants, who were interviewed using semi-structured interviews. Results: The findings showed that 38.7% of participants scored emotional problems above the normal range. In the same range, but with different % is also conduct problems 84.6%, hyperactivity 73.6% and peer problems 93.2%. Qualitative findings highlighted difficulties in identifying the early signs of psychological problems and emphasized the important role of families, teachers, and peers in helping children and adolescents cope with psychological difficulties. Conclusion: The findings indicate a clear need to increase public awareness of psychological problems, as well as to strengthen professional mental health services. Furthermore, there is a need to create supportive environments within families and schools that encourage open discussion of psychosocial difficulties and promote early identification and intervention.

title: Fertility care for transgender and gender diverse individuals in Germany: an interview study with healthcare providers on the importance of care, care provision, barriers, and improvement strategies.
abstract: As gender-affirming care can impact fertility in transgender and gender diverse individuals (TGDI), fertility preservation (FP) may help TGDI to have biological children in the future. The reported discrepancy between the proportion of TGDI who express a desire to have biological children (up to 50%) and low FP utilization rates (3-10%) highlights the need for high-quality fertility care, including fertility related counseling and the provision of FP. However, there is limited knowledge of the extent to which fertility care is being offered in Germany. Therefore, this study aims to examine the current state of fertility care for TGDI in Germany from the perspective of healthcare providers. We conducted 30 semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers from various somatic and mental healthcare disciplines caring for TGDI in Germany. The interview guide addressed four topics of interest: the importance of care, care provision, barriers to care, and improvement strategies. The interviews were transcribed and analyzed using structuring qualitative content analysis by Kuckartz. Deductive and inductive coding were applied to identify main and subcategories from the interviews. Almost all interviewees considered fertility care for TGDI to be highly important and believed that fertility counseling should be an integral part of care, while they highlighted that the importance of FP depended on the individual family planning desires and life circumstances of TGDI. Most interviewees routinely provided fertility counseling prior to gender-affirming care. We identified several barriers to fertility care for TGDI in Germany: TGDI-related (knowledge gaps, low priority of FP, dysphoria), healthcare provider-related (lack of knowledge, experience, gender sensitivity), procedural (invasiveness of FP, dysphoria triggers), structural (inadequate healthcare infrastructure, research, costs), legal (historic requirement of infertility, prohibition of surrogacy and egg donation), and societal (discrimination, cis- and heteronormative image of family life). To address these barriers, the interviewees suggested promoting healthcare providers' competence, further research and guidelines, standardizing fertility counseling, enhancing interdisciplinary cooperation, ensuring transparency of services, routine cost coverage of FP, and promoting societal acceptance. According to the interviewees, optimized fertility care for TGDI requires healthcare provider training, standardized fertility counseling, stronger interdisciplinary cooperation, regular cost coverage of FP, and societal education. Our findings can help inform the development of clinical guidelines. Future quantitative data on care provision and research on the perspectives of TGDI themselves are essential to obtain a comprehensive understanding of fertility care for TGDI in Germany. Our study was approved by the Hamburg Medical Council ("Ärztekammer Hamburg") for conduct as a "scientific case" (2023-300381-WF, September 11th, 2023).

title: The Evolved Nest in Childhood: Relation to Adult Well-being and Social Capital Across Cultures
abstract: Evolved nests are species-specific developmental systems that support biological, psychological, and social needs. The human evolved nest includes practices such as responsive care, self-directed play, and extensive affectionate touch. Previous studies have linked childhood experience of these practices to both child and adult well-being. Here we assessed whether recall of evolved nest experiences during childhood (age 0–18) was related to three dimensions of adult well-being and social capital (personal well-being, social relationships, and general prosociality) in three countries (USA, UK, Japan). Recalled evolved nest experience was positively associated with multiple measures under each dimension across cultures after controlling for demographic factors (n = 1,401). In contrast, it was not found to be associated with incentivised measures of prosociality (elicited via a series of economic games) in any country. Exploratory factor analyses revealed that experiences of evolved nest practices clustered together under two common factors in each country: positive and negative experiences. These factors were independently associated with multiple indicators of adult well-being and social capital in each country, and these associations were generally stronger for positive (vs. negative) experiences. Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that childhood experience of the evolved nest has long-term benefits for individual and societal well-being regardless of cultural differences.

title: Timmy’s Trip to Planet Earth: The Long-Term Effects of a Social and Emotional Education Program for Preschool Children
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Social and Emotional Education (SEE) interventions during early childhood have shown considerable promise in enhancing children's emotion understanding, social competence, and behavioural adjustments. However, few studies have examined their long-term impact, especially across the preschool-to-primary school transition. This study evaluated the effectiveness of a manualized SEE program, Timmy's Trip to Planet Earth, in promoting emotional, behavioural, and social functioning over time. METHODS: A quasi-experimental longitudinal design was adopted with pre- and post-test assessments conducted approximately 18 months apart. Participants were 89 typically developing children (aged 59-71 months), assigned to an experimental group (n = 45) or a waiting-list group (n = 44). The program combined teacher training, classroom-based lessons, home activities, and teachers' ongoing implementation support. The effectiveness of the program was measured via the Test of Emotion Comprehension (TEC), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and the Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation (SCBE-30). RESULTS: Significant Time × Group interactions were observed for the TEC External and Mental components, indicating greater improvements in emotion recognition and mental state understanding in the intervention group. The SDQ revealed significant reductions in conduct problems and increased prosocial behaviours. In the SCBE-30, a significant interaction effect was found for social competence, with the intervention group showing greater improvement over time compared to the control group. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that SEE programs can produce meaningful and lasting improvements in children's emotional and social skills across key educational transitions. Teacher training and family involvement likely played a critical role in supporting the program's sustained impact.

title: Platform Growth Is Hard: Experimental and Quasi‐Experimental Evidence From a Carpooling Platform in Singapore
abstract: We study platform growth in a field experiment with drivers on a peer‐to‐peer carpooling platform in Singapore. Motivated by both theory and observed practice, we ask whether temporary subsidies and informational campaigns can have durable effects on the growth of platforms. Drivers were randomly assigned to different standard promotional strategies: some drivers receive information about favorable market conditions, others receive subsidies for picking up passengers. Informational nudges re‐engage dormant drivers in the short run, but the effect is temporary and does not generate durable market growth. While subsidies may generate a small initial increase in participation, they reduce participation in the longer term. Estimating drivers' preferences, we find that drivers may adjust their selectivity when they know they are scarce relative to passengers—an equilibrium response in matching markets that explains why, in settings with multidimensional preferences, standard promotional strategies may fail to generate durable growth.

title: Motor Synchrony, Social Learning and Closeness in Group Play Settings
abstract: Playful activities provide critical opportunities for rhythmic interactions, which may affect social and cognitive development in early childhood. Prior research suggests that motor synchrony promotes closeness and prosocial behaviour, but few studies have examined its role in social learning. This study investigated whether motor synchrony, through a clapping game, enhances preschoolers' closeness with others, imitation, over-imitation, and prosociality. We hypothesized that children would feel closer, imitate more, and share more with a partner who moved in synchrony compared to one who moved asynchronously. In a group setting, motor synchrony and asynchrony were experimentally induced between the child and two experimenters. Bayesian analyses revealed no credible evidence for differences in affiliation, imitation, over-imitation, or prosocial behaviour between experimenters (BF10=0.045-0.216). A manipulation check indicated low motor synchrony scores, suggesting the intended synchrony may not have been fully achieved, potentially influencing the outcomes. These findings highlight the challenges of inducing motor synchrony in playful group contexts and raise questions about the conditions necessary for synchrony to impact social learning in young children.

title: How does social media reshape virtual acculturation? A game-mediated framework for cross-cultural adaptation.
abstract: This study examines the social and cultural significance of video games as a major form of entertainment among contemporary youth and investigates how social media-mediated game video consumption shapes the interpretation of foreign game cultures. Drawing on a dataset of game videos and 78,169 Danmaku comments from the Chinese social media platform Bilibili, this study employs a multimodal analytical approach integrating natural language processing (NLP), data modeling, and manual coding to explore how culturally salient meanings are identified, elaborated, and circulated in social media interaction. Building on Kim's ITCCA framework, the study proposes a game virtual acculturation framework consisting of three interrelated dimensions: cultural understanding of game content, cultural behavior through vicarious learning, and cultural identity of social media. At the micro level, the analysis focuses on Danmaku interactions triggered by in-game content and identifies the cultural elements that most frequently organize players' interpretations. At the meso level, time-series analysis traces the dynamic development of cultural information in Danmaku commentary and shows how observational engagement supports the accumulation of cultural knowledge in social media environments. At the macro level, the study demonstrates how individual gameplay-related responses are reorganized into more collectively framed cultural interpretations through video sharing and public discussion, revealing recurrent patterns of shared meaning-making in the negotiation of foreign game culture. Taken together, these findings extend ITCCA into the context of digital entertainment and contribute a framework for understanding virtual acculturation through game-related social media.

title: Effective altruism, technoscience and the making of philanthropic value
abstract: A recent philanthropic movement with advocates among high-profile tech entrepreneurs and philosophers, effective altruism (EA) has been widely disparaged for its flawed moral philosophy and conservative political implications. As philanthropic practice, however, it has been seldom studied. In this paper, we argue that claims to technoscientific expertise are central to how EA actors understand, legitimize, and take part in the production of philanthropic value. We analyze their practices of categorization, ranking and measurement as well as underlying technoscientific imaginaries and moral views through comparing three areas of EA intervention: neglected tropical diseases, cultured meat, and AI safety. We show how EA involves various and contested ambitions to direct knowledge production and redraw the boundaries of expert communities, shedding light on the centrality of technoscience in philanthropists' worldmaking ambitions.

title: Family events and child behavior in late childhood: a cross-sectional study.
abstract: Children's social behavior develops through diverse experiences. However, the relationship between children's experiences of celebratory events and their behavioral development has not been previously quantified. Therefore, this study aimed to quantitatively explore this relationship. In 2020, a self-reported questionnaire was completed by 653 sixth-grade students (aged 11-12 years) and/or their caregivers in Nagoya, Aichi, a major metropolitan area in Japan. The main items surveyed were children's experiences with events celebrated by their family and their behavioral development. The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire was used to assess children's behavior. This questionnaire identifies behavioral and emotional problems and prosocial behavior. Multiple regression analysis was conducted with the number of family events experienced by children as the explanatory variable and their emotional and prosocial behavior as the objective variables. Children from families who participated in fewer family events tended to have higher problematic behavior risk scores and lower prosociality scores compared with their counterparts. Compared with children who participated in more than 20 family events, those who participated in fewer than 10 family events had more than three times the risk for exhibiting problem behaviors (odds: 3.558, 95% CI: 1.252-10.111, p = .017) and prosocial problems (odds: 3.184, 95% CI: 1.726-5.876, p < .001). Conversely, children from families who participated in more family events tended to have lower problematic behavior risk scores and higher prosociality scores. A higher number of family events may reduce the risk of behavioral problems in children and increase their prosociality. Enjoying family events may be beneficial for social adjustment.

title: Hubungan Antara Kebersyukuran Dan Perilaku Prososial Dimediasi Meaning In Life Pada Relawan Pendidikan
abstract: Penelitian mengenai kebersyukuran, meaning in life, dan perilaku prososial pada relawan pendidikan di wilayah dengan keterbatasan akses pendidikan masih perlu dikaji lebih lanjut. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui hubungan antara kebersyukuran dan perilaku prososial yang dimediasi oleh meaning in life. Partisipan penelitian berjumlah 398 relawan pendidikan yang pernah melaksanakan kegiatan kerelawanan selama 1–2 minggu di wilayah dengan keterbatasan akses pendidikan dan dipilih menggunakan teknik purposive sampling. Data dikumpulkan menggunakan skala kebersyukuran, Prosocialness for Adult (PSA), dan Meaning in Life Questionnaire (MLQ). Analisis data menggunakan korelasi Spearman-Rank dan analisis mediasi PROCESS Macro Model 4 secara terpisah untuk dimensi presence of meaning dan search for meaning, dengan bootstrapping 5.000 sampel dan tingkat kepercayaan 95%. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa kebersyukuran berhubungan positif dan signifikan dengan perilaku prososial (rₛ = 0,124; p = 0,013) dan presence of meaning (rₛ = 0,285; p < 0,001), tetapi tidak dengan search for meaning (rₛ = −0,028; p = 0,574). Presence of meaning dan search for meaning berhubungan positif dan signifikan dengan perilaku prososial (rₛ = 0,188; p < 0,001 dan rₛ = 0,321; p < 0,001). Analisis mediasi menunjukkan bahwa presence of meaning memediasi hubungan kebersyukuran dan perilaku prososial (efek tidak langsung = 0,0136; 95% CI [0,0044; 0,0248]), sedangkan search for meaning tidak memediasi hubungan tersebut (efek tidak langsung = 0,0019; 95% CI [−0,0077; 0,0120]). Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa peran meaning in life dalam hubungan tersebut berbeda berdasarkan dimensinya.

title: Exploring Donor Giving, Intent, and Expectations of Disaster Relief Nonprofits: The Kangaroo Island Bushfire Case
abstract: In response to concerns regarding how disaster relief nonprofit organizations distribute financial donations, this paper explores individual donor giving, intent upon giving, and expectations subsequent to giving, in the context of the 2019/20 Kangaroo Island bushfires in South Australia. Adopting fundamental constructs from the theory of planned behavior, we examine why people give to natural disaster fundraising campaigns. We then compare donor intent and their expectations of nonprofits subsequent to giving, with nonprofits' actions and communication to consider how (un/met) expectations might impact on attitudes to future giving. A qualitative approach was adopted involving 14 semi‐structured interviews with individual donors (most of whom were geographically close to the disaster location), publicly available communication regarding the disaster, and e‐mail correspondence with the relevant nonprofits. Findings reveal the importance of closeness (geographical, emotional and psychological) to a range of factors influencing giving behavior. Contrary to extant literature that cautions a misalignment between donors' intent, expectations, and nonprofits' actions, this occurrence did not impact negatively on donors' satisfaction or attitudes towards future giving behavior. Implications extend to better understanding why donors give, their expectations following a natural disaster, and the multiple dimensions of donor closeness.
